name: Chilli Bell Lantern
summary: Mild-to-medium heat, bell-shaped fruit, 1–1.5 m tall. A long-lived perennial in frost-free peninsula gardens.

cautions.text: Wear gloves when handling or cutting hot fruit, and keep hands away from eyes.

glance.indoors: Possible on a sunny enclosed verandah

growing: 6+ hours of sun, sheltered from salty north-easterlies.
Rich and free-draining, pH 6–7. Dig compost and aged manure into peninsula sand; apply wetting agent.
Deeply 2–3 times a week in summer and mulch well. Erratic watering causes flower drop.
Potassium-rich liquid feed (tomato food) every 2 weeks once flowering. Go easy on nitrogen.
Hand-pollinate every couple of days while flowering.
Queensland fruit fly (bag or net fruit from December), aphids, whitefly.
Cut back by a third in late autumn; it regrows in spring.
harvest: From about 90 days. Pick green or wait for full red colour; regular picking keeps it producing.
uses: Fruity flavour. Stuff whole, or use in salsas, chilli jam and pickles.
Capsaicin is used in warming rubs.
Ornamental fruit; looks great in a large pot.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · liquid feed every 2nd Sunday · fruit fly check on the 1st, Dec–Apr · stake 6 Dec · hand-pollinate if indoors · prune back mid-May.

name: Chilli Long Red
summary: Cayenne-type chilli, medium-hot, 60–90 cm tall. Crops heavily through summer and autumn.

cautions.text: Wear gloves when handling or cutting hot fruit, and keep hands away from eyes.

growing: Full sun, warm and sheltered from salt wind.
Rich and well-drained, pH 6–7. Improve peninsula sand with compost and manure.
Keep evenly moist; let the top 2 cm dry between waterings. Mulch.
Potassium-rich liquid feed every 2 weeks from first flowers.
Pinch out the first few flowers for a bushier, more productive plant.
A single stake once laden with fruit.
Hand-pollinate every couple of days while flowering.
Overwinters outdoors on the peninsula if pruned back; crops best in its first two years.
harvest: From 70–90 days. Snip with scissors rather than pulling. Red fruit is hotter and sweeter than green.
uses: Stir-fries, curries, hot sauce. Dries well for flakes and powder.
Warming rubs; blended chilli-garlic spray deters chewing insects.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · liquid feed every 2nd Sunday · fruit fly check on the 1st, Dec–Apr · stake 6 Dec · hand-pollinate if indoors · prune back mid-May.

name: Self Heal
summary: Low spreading groundcover, 10–30 cm, with purple flower spikes from late spring to autumn. Very easy.
growing: Part shade is ideal; full sun only if kept moist.
Moisture-retentive. Add plenty of compost to peninsula sand so it doesn't dry out.
Keep consistently moist; it wilts fast in hot, dry spells.
A handful of compost in spring is enough.
Spreads by creeping stems. Trim after flowering for a tidy plant and a second flush.
Divide clumps in autumn or spring.
harvest: Pick leaves and flowering tops in summer while in bloom.
uses: Young leaves in salads or cooked as greens.
Used as a mouthwash, gargle and wash for minor wounds.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · indoor check Tue and Sat if potted inside.

name: Calendula
summary: Pot marigold. Annual, 40–60 cm, with orange or yellow edible flowers. Flowers best in cooler months but carries on into early summer.

cautions.text: Avoid if allergic to daisy-family plants.

growing: Full sun; afternoon shade helps it last into summer.
Average, well-drained. Copes with sandy peninsula soil.
Moderate. Water at the base to avoid mildew.
Light liquid feed once a month.
Pick spent flowers every few days to keep it blooming.
Powdery mildew in humid weather. Improve airflow and remove affected leaves.
Let a few heads set seed; it self-sows for an autumn crop.
harvest: Pick fully open flowers in the morning. Dry petals on paper in the shade.
uses: Petals in salads, rice, butter and as a garnish.
Infused oil and balms for dry skin, minor cuts and nappy rash.
Draws hoverflies and bees; acts as a trap crop for aphids near the chillies.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · deadhead Saturdays · snail checks to mid-Nov · save seed 7 Feb.

name: Lemon Balm
summary: Lemon-scented mint relative forming a bushy clump 50–80 cm tall. Hardy and fast-growing.

cautions.text: Can upset cats' and dogs' stomachs if eaten.
Check with a GP before medicinal use if pregnant or on thyroid or sedative medication.

growing: Morning sun and afternoon shade; leaves scorch in harsh summer afternoons. Shelter from salt wind.
Moist and fertile. Add compost to sandy soil.
Regularly in warm weather; tolerates short dry spells once established.
Compost in spring only; heavy feeding weakens the flavour.
Cut back by half in midsummer and again in late autumn.
Self-seeds heavily. Trim off flowers before they set seed.
Pinch tips often to keep it compact.
harvest: Pick leaves any time; best flavour just before flowering. Use fresh, or dry quickly in shade.
uses: Tea, desserts, salads, cordials and iced water.
Calming tea for stress, sleep and an upset stomach.
Strong bee attractant; the name Melissa means honey bee.
Check with a GP before medicinal use if pregnant or on thyroid or sedative medication.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · pinch tips Saturdays · cut back 10 Jan and 9 May · indoor check Tue and Sat if potted inside.

name: French Lavender
summary: Toothed grey-green leaves and flowers almost year-round; grows to about 1 m. Handles humidity and salty coastal air better than English lavender.

cautions.text: Can upset cats' and dogs' stomachs if eaten. Keep lavender oil away from pets.

growing: Full sun and good airflow. A good windbreak for the windward side of the garden.
Sharply drained, slightly alkaline. Peninsula sand suits it; add a little garden lime. No rich compost.
In low spots near Brisbane Water that stay wet after rain, plant on a mound or raised bed.
Water in well for the first month, then only when dry. Wet roots are the main cause of death.
Rarely; a light sprinkle of slow-release in spring at most.
Trim lightly after each flush, removing spent spikes and a few cm of foliage. Never cut into bare old wood.
Gravel, or keep organic mulch well away from the stem.
harvest: Cut stems when flowers are just opening; hang upside down in bunches to dry.
uses: Flowers sparingly in baking and syrups; stronger and more camphor-like than English lavender.
Dried sachets, bath soaks, linen spray and potpourri.
Bees and butterflies; a hardy low hedge.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri only if dry · trim 17 Jan and 18 Apr · spring soil prep each September.

name: Hops
summary: Vigorous climbing vine growing 4–6 m a season; dies back in winter and reshoots in spring. Peninsula winters are mild, so expect a lighter cone crop than cooler areas.

cautions.text: Toxic to dogs, even dried or spent hops from brewing. Fence it off and keep dogs away from fallen cones.
Adds to the effect of sedatives and alcohol; check with a GP before medicinal use.

growing: Full sun with tall support: a pergola, fence, or strings up to an eave. Shelter from salt wind.
Deep and rich. Dig plenty of compost and manure into the sand.
Deeply 2–3 times a week in summer; mulch thickly.
Nitrogen-rich feed in spring for growth, then balanced feed from midsummer. Feed little and often in sandy soil.
Choose 2–4 strong shoots and wind them clockwise around the support; remove the rest.
Aphids and two-spotted mites in hot, dry weather.
Cut dead bines to ground level once they brown off.
harvest: Late summer to early autumn, when cones feel papery and leave yellow lupulin powder on your fingers.
uses: Young spring shoots cooked like asparagus.
Beer brewing; dried cones in sleep pillows or tea.
Fast summer screen over a pergola or fence.
Toxic to dogs. Adds to the effect of sedatives and alcohol; check with a GP before medicinal use.
reminders: Train bines 1 Nov · water Mon/Wed/Fri · liquid feed every 2nd Sunday · cone checks weekly from 21 Feb · cut back 6 Jun.

name: Toothache Plant
summary: Paracress or buzz buttons. Sprawling plant 30–40 cm tall with gold-and-red button flowers that make your mouth tingle and go numb.

cautions.text: Strong numbing effect. Avoid in pregnancy and with daisy-family allergies; supervise children.

growing: Full sun to part shade; loves warm, humid summers. Shelter from salt wind.
Rich and moist. Sandy soil needs lots of compost to hold water.
Never let it dry out; it wilts quickly.
Balanced liquid feed every 2–3 weeks in summer.
Pinch tips to keep it bushy.
Frost-free on the peninsula, so it may carry on as a short-lived perennial in a sheltered spot.
Save seed from dried heads or take tip cuttings in autumn as backup.
harvest: Pick flower buds and leaves as needed through summer and autumn.
uses: Leaves and flowers add a tingle to salads, cocktails and Brazilian dishes such as tacacá.
Flower buds chewed to numb toothache and sore gums.
Striking bullseye flowers; good in hanging baskets.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · liquid feed every 2nd Sunday · pinch tips Saturdays · seed and cuttings 11 Apr · indoor check Tue and Sat if potted inside.

name: Echinacea Purpurea
summary: Purple coneflower. Clumping perennial 60–100 cm tall with pink-purple daisies in summer. May flower lightly in its first season while it establishes.

cautions.text: Avoid with daisy-family allergies or autoimmune conditions; check with a GP before medicinal use.

growing: 6+ hours of sun. Shade gives floppy stems and few flowers.
Well-drained, average fertility. Sandy soil is fine with a little compost.
Raise beds in low, soggy spots; wet winter soil causes crown rot.
Regularly for the first couple of months, then drought-tolerant.
Deadhead to extend flowering; leave late heads for birds. Cut to the ground in late autumn; it reshoots in spring.
Snails and slugs on young shoots in the first few weeks.
harvest: Flowers and leaves in summer. Roots are usually dug from plants 3+ years old, in autumn.
uses: Tea or tincture from roots, leaves and flowers, taken at the first signs of a cold.
Long-lasting cut flower; seed heads feed finches.
Avoid with daisy-family allergies or autoimmune conditions; check with a GP first.
reminders: Snail checks to mid-Nov · water Mon/Wed/Fri only if dry · deadhead Saturdays · cut back 16 May.

name: Valerian
summary: Leafy clump that sends up flower stalks to 1–1.5 m with fragrant white-pink flowers in summer.

cautions.text: Adds to the effect of sedatives and alcohol. Check with a GP before use, especially if pregnant.

growing: Sun to part shade; afternoon shade helps on hot westerly days.
Moist, rich and loamy. Sandy peninsula soil needs heavy compost and mulch to hold moisture.
Compost or balanced feed in spring.
Stake tall flower stems in windy spots. Remove flower heads before seeding unless you want it spreading.
Divide clumps in autumn or spring.
harvest: Dig roots in the second autumn (around April 2028), wash and dry. Replant a division to keep it going.
uses: Root tea or tincture as a sleep aid.
Fragrant flowers for bees and butterflies. Cats love the dried root.
Adds to the effect of sedatives and alcohol. Check with a GP before use, especially if pregnant.

name: Comfrey
summary: Big deep-rooted perennial up to 1 m with large hairy leaves and bell flowers. The gardener's fertiliser plant.

cautions.text: Not for eating or tea: it contains liver-toxic alkaloids. Leaf hairs irritate skin, so wear gloves.
Toxic to pets and livestock if eaten; keep away from grazing animals.

growing: Choose its spot permanently; any root fragment left behind regrows. Tough enough to shelter other plants from salt wind.
Almost any. Grows biggest in rich, moist soil.
Regular in summer; deep roots make it tough once established.
harvest: Cut leaves 5 cm above ground once about 60 cm tall; it regrows for 3–5 cuts a season. Wear gloves; the hairs irritate skin.
uses: Not for eating or tea. It contains liver-toxic alkaloids.
Ointments and poultices for bruises and sprains, on unbroken skin only.
Steep leaves in water 4–6 weeks for liquid fertiliser (dilute 1:10). Chop-and-drop mulch and compost activator, great for feeding hungry peninsula sand.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · cut leaves every 6 weeks from 13 Dec.

name: Yarrow White
summary: Feathery leaves and flat white flower heads on 50–90 cm stems from late spring to autumn. Tough and low-maintenance.

cautions.text: Can upset cats' and dogs' stomachs and skin if eaten.
Avoid in pregnancy and with daisy-family allergies.

growing: Full sun. Handles heat, wind and salt; a good front-line plant near the beach.
Poor to average and well-drained. Peninsula sand suits it; rich soil makes it floppy.
Water in for a few weeks, then very drought-tolerant.
Deadhead to prolong flowering; cut back to the leafy base after flowering.
Spreads by underground runners. Divide every 2–3 years in spring.
harvest: Cut flowers and leaves when blooms are fully open; dry in bunches.
uses: Applied to minor cuts to slow bleeding; tea for colds.
Draws ladybirds and hoverflies that eat aphids, so plant near the chillies. Also a compost activator.
Avoid in pregnancy and with daisy-family allergies.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri only if dry · deadhead Saturdays · spring soil prep each September.

name: Lemongrass
summary: Dense grassy clump up to 1–1.5 m tall and wide. Thrives in warm, frost-free peninsula summers.

cautions.text: Leaf edges are sharp; wear gloves when cutting.
Can upset cats' and dogs' stomachs if eaten in quantity.

growing: Rich and moist. Dig compost and manure into sandy soil.
Regularly through summer; much less in winter.
Nitrogen-rich feed (pelleted chicken manure) every 4–6 weeks in the growing season.
Cut the whole clump back to about 20 cm in late winter. Divide every 2–3 years.
Leaf edges are sharp; wear gloves.
harvest: After about 3 months, snap or cut outer stalks at the base once 1–2 cm thick. Use the pale lower stem; leaves make tea.
uses: Thai and Vietnamese curries, soups, marinades and tea. Freezes well.
Clumping screen; cut leaves make mulch.
reminders: Water Mon/Wed/Fri · liquid feed every 2nd Sunday · cut back 22 Aug.
